sections.title: Stabilization first
sections.text: Assess circulating-volume loss and instability before etiologic classification or outpatient treatment.

sections.title: Initial treatment
sections.text: When appropriate, begin medical therapy chosen around contraindications; PALM-COEIN organizes the causes after stabilization.

sections.title: Escalation and maintenance
sections.text: Instability, medical contraindications or treatment failure warrant surgical consideration; controlled bleeding needs a maintenance plan.

sections.title: Match the test to its purpose
sections.text: Endometrial biopsy obtains uterine lining for microscopic examination. Hysteroscopy directly examines the uterine cavity. These are diagnostic options, not a requirement that every patient receive every procedure.

sections.title: Evaluate the consequence of prolonged blood loss
sections.text: Heavy menstrual blood loss can cause iron deficiency. CBC and hemoglobin assess anemia, while iron and ferritin help assess iron deficiency. This reference supplies no biopsy age cutoff or ferritin diagnostic threshold.

sections.title: Adult diagnostic approach
sections.text: After excluding other causes, adult ovulatory dysfunction plus hyperandrogenism can establish diagnosis without ovarian ultrasound or AMH.

sections.title: Broader risk assessment
sections.text: The syndrome also warrants assessment of glycemic, cardiovascular and psychological risks; reproductive symptoms are only part of its burden.

sections.title: Anovulatory infertility
sections.text: Letrozole is the preferred initial ovulation-induction drug when anovulation is the only infertility factor; exclude pregnancy first.

sections.title: Treatment when pregnancy is not desired
sections.text: NICHD describes combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptives as a primary long-term option for PCOS symptoms in women with intact ovaries who do not want pregnancy. They can improve irregular cycles and androgen-related symptoms; suitability and contraindications still matter.

sections.title: Address metabolic health alongside symptoms
sections.text: For PCOS with overweight or obesity, increased physical activity and modest weight loss can improve symptoms, insulin and cholesterol levels, and sometimes ovulation. This does not guarantee pregnancy or replace individualized symptom treatment.

choices.text: Both ultrasound and AMH
Ovarian biopsy

questions.explanation: Adult ovulatory dysfunction and hyperandrogenism make additional ovarian morphology testing unnecessary.

distractorExplanations.A: Combining both is not required.
distractorExplanations.B: Biopsy is not a diagnostic requirement.
distractorExplanations.D: These two features already satisfy criteria.
distractorExplanations.E: AMH is unnecessary in this presentation.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid unnecessary ovarian testing in an adult meeting clinical criteria.

Letrozole
Metformin as the preferred ovulation agent

questions.explanation: The guideline prefers letrozole for isolated anovulatory infertility.

distractorExplanations.A: This does not induce ovulation for conception.
distractorExplanations.B: Letrozole is the preferred initial agent.
distractorExplanations.C: Effective induction treatment is available.
distractorExplanations.E: More effective induction agents are available.

questions.learningObjective: Identify first-line induction for isolated PCOS anovulation.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old with established PCOS has irregular cycles, acne and unwanted hair growth. She has intact ovaries, does not want pregnancy, and has no contraindication to estrogen. Which long-term option addresses these symptoms?

choices.text: Ovulation induction intended to achieve pregnancy
Hair-removal treatment without a menstrual management plan
Intermittent progestin courses as the entire plan for acne and unwanted hair
A combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive
An androgen-focused treatment plan that leaves cycle irregularity unaddressed

questions.explanation: NICHD describes combined oral contraceptives as a primary long-term option in this reproductive context, with improved cycle regularity and androgen-related symptoms. The scenario explicitly supplies absence of an estrogen contraindication.

distractorExplanations.A: The patient is not seeking pregnancy; NICHD describes a different primary long-term option for this symptom pattern.
distractorExplanations.B: It does not address the combined menstrual and androgen-related goals specified.
distractorExplanations.C: This is not the combined estrogen-progestin approach that NICHD describes for the supplied goals.
distractorExplanations.E: The question calls for a long-term option addressing both menstrual irregularity and androgen-related symptoms.

questions.learningObjective: Match PCOS symptom therapy to reproductive goals.

questions.stem: A patient with PCOS, overweight and insulin resistance is receiving appropriate menstrual symptom treatment. What is the most appropriate additional counseling focus?

choices.text: Discuss activity and weight only after infertility treatment fails
A feasible physical-activity and modest weight-loss plan
Limit counseling to cosmetic hair and acne concerns
Set weight loss as a guarantee of future fertility
Withhold menstrual symptom care until a target weight is reached

questions.explanation: NICHD reports benefits of physical activity and modest weight loss for PCOS when overweight or obesity is present, including improved insulin and cholesterol levels and possible restoration of ovulation.

distractorExplanations.A: The reference describes metabolic benefits in the current overweight, insulin-resistant context, without requiring infertility treatment first.
distractorExplanations.C: It omits the metabolic concerns explicitly supplied in the vignette.
distractorExplanations.D: NICHD describes possible benefits rather than a guaranteed reproductive outcome.
distractorExplanations.E: The source supports lifestyle measures as part of care; it does not require withholding the current symptom plan.

questions.learningObjective: Integrate metabolic counseling into PCOS study cases.

limitations: International 2023 guideline with US ASRM participation; current ASRM page uses PMOS nomenclature. Recommendations cited here concern adults, not adolescent diagnostic thresholds.

sections.title: Vasomotor treatment
sections.text: Systemic hormone therapy effectively treats bothersome hot flashes; decisions account for timing, contraindications and preferences.

sections.title: Endometrial protection
sections.text: An intact uterus generally requires adequate progestogen with systemic estrogen; conjugated estrogen/bazedoxifene is a specified exception.

sections.title: Local symptoms
sections.text: Low-dose vaginal estrogen targets genitourinary symptoms; it differs from systemic treatment and generally does not require added progestogen.

sections.title: Nonhormonal symptom options
sections.text: The MedlinePlus summary lists certain antidepressants among nonhormonal medication options for hot flashes. Medication selection depends on history, preferences and risks; this section does not specify a particular drug or dose.

sections.title: A behavioral option for sleep symptoms
sections.text: MedlinePlus lists cognitive behavioral therapy for trouble sleeping during the menopausal transition, alongside sleep habits such as a cool, dark and quiet bedroom. Treating insomnia does not require that every patient choose hormone therapy.

distractorExplanations.D: Uterine status remains relevant.

distractorExplanations.D: The vignette identifies no infection.
distractorExplanations.E: Effective symptom-directed options exist.

sections.title: Treatment goals
sections.text: Treatment selection depends on pain burden and fertility goals; symptom control does not represent a permanent cure.

sections.title: Hormonal suppression
sections.text: Hormonal treatment can reduce pain. An appropriate progestin-only contraceptive formulation can address pain and contraception when estrogen is unsuitable; absent menstruation alone does not ensure pregnancy prevention.

sections.title: Counseling about recurrence
sections.text: Symptoms may return after hormonal treatment stops or after surgery; treatment and fertility planning need individualized discussion.

sections.title: Interpret normal imaging cautiously
sections.text: NICHD describes ultrasound and MRI as useful for locating larger endometriosis lesions, nodules or cysts, while small lesions and adhesions may not be demonstrated. Normal imaging alone therefore cannot establish absence of endometriosis.

sections.title: What a surgical assessment can provide
sections.text: When laparoscopy is chosen after evaluation, it permits direct inspection for endometriosis and sometimes tissue biopsy for microscopy. This older clinical reference is not used to require surgery before symptom treatment or to impose a current universal diagnostic pathway.

questions.stem: A patient with established endometriosis seeks hormonal pain suppression and contraception. Estrogen is unsuitable because of high thrombotic risk. Which option fits this goal?

choices.text: An ovulation-induction drug
An appropriate progestin-only contraceptive formulation
Estrogen despite the contraindication
An antibiotic for suppression
A promise of permanent cure

questions.explanation: NIH lists progestin-only contraceptive options when estrogen is unsuitable; contraceptive choice must be explicit rather than inferred from menstrual suppression.

distractorExplanations.A: She is seeking suppression, not conception.
distractorExplanations.C: The stated risk makes estrogen unsuitable.
distractorExplanations.D: No infection is identified.
distractorExplanations.E: Suppression does not guarantee cure.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize an estrogen-free option for endometriosis pain suppression.

questions.stem: A patient improved with hormonal treatment for endometriosis but asks whether stopping it guarantees permanent pain relief. What is the most accurate counseling?

choices.text: Recurrence proves the original diagnosis was wrong
Fertility goals never affect treatment
Symptoms may recur after treatment stops
Hormonal therapy permanently cures all disease
Treatment eliminates every existing adhesion

questions.explanation: Symptom relief during suppression does not assure durable remission after stopping therapy.

distractorExplanations.A: Recurrence is compatible with endometriosis.
distractorExplanations.B: Reproductive goals influence treatment selection.
distractorExplanations.D: Permanent cure is not established.
distractorExplanations.E: Hormonal suppression does not remove existing adhesions.

questions.learningObjective: Set appropriate expectations about hormonal symptom control.

questions.stem: A patient has symptoms concerning for endometriosis, but pelvic imaging shows no large lesion. What is the most appropriate interpretation of the imaging result?

choices.text: Small endometriosis lesions may still be present
A negative imaging result excludes even very small lesions
MRI is guaranteed to exclude all lesions missed by ultrasound
Symptoms alone confirm the diagnosis once imaging is negative
Further assessment is unnecessary until infertility occurs

questions.explanation: NICHD describes an imaging limitation for small lesions and adhesions. This item tests interpretation, not a rule requiring laparoscopy in every symptomatic patient.

distractorExplanations.B: NICHD identifies small-lesion limitations of imaging, so this conclusion is too strong.
distractorExplanations.C: The reference does not provide that guarantee; it describes limits in detecting small lesions.
distractorExplanations.D: The imaging limitation preserves diagnostic uncertainty rather than establishing the diagnosis from symptoms alone.
distractorExplanations.E: The cited imaging limitation does not justify ending the assessment of the current symptoms.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid ruling out endometriosis solely because imaging is unrevealing.

questions.stem: After evaluation and discussion of options, a patient elects laparoscopic assessment of suspected endometriosis. Which added finding can provide tissue confirmation of an observed lesion?

choices.text: Visual inspection without sampling an observed lesion
MRI appearance of the pelvis alone
A record of symptom response to treatment alone
Microscopic examination of a lesion biopsy
A serum marker result without sampling the lesion

questions.explanation: NICHD describes tissue biopsy during some laparoscopic procedures to help confirm endometriosis. The scenario supplies an elected surgical assessment rather than requiring surgery for all suspected cases.

distractorExplanations.A: The question asks for tissue confirmation, which requires a specimen rather than visual inspection alone.
distractorExplanations.B: It does not provide the microscopic examination of a lesion specimen described by NICHD.
distractorExplanations.C: It does not provide histologic confirmation of the observed lesion.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not provide the tissue microscopy specifically requested.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the role of lesion histology during selected surgical evaluation.

limitations: NIH official informational reference, not a formal guideline. The March 2026 ACOG diagnostic guideline and February 2026 official announcement were inaccessible and are not used as evidence. ESHRE 2022 was verified on its official site but excluded because its PDF prohibits commercial use without permission.

sections.title: Presumptive diagnosis
sections.text: STI risk, unexplained pelvic pain and cervical-motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness support prompt presumptive treatment.

sections.title: Outpatient coverage
sections.text: For suitable mild-to-moderate disease, ceftriaxone plus doxycycline and metronidazole covers common organisms, including anaerobes.

sections.title: Failure to improve
sections.text: Failure to improve within 72 hours of outpatient treatment warrants hospitalization, regimen review and additional diagnostic evaluation.

sections.title: Pregnancy changes the setting
sections.text: Pregnant patients suspected of having PID should be hospitalized and receive IV antimicrobial treatment in consultation with an infectious disease specialist. This is distinct from ordinary outpatient management of mild-to-moderate nonpregnant PID.

sections.title: An IUD need not be removed immediately
sections.text: For an IUD user with PID, treat appropriately and provide close follow-up; immediate device removal is not required. Consider removal if there is no improvement after 48–72 hours. The evidence reviewed by CDC mainly involved copper or other nonhormonal devices.

distractorExplanations.E: It omits required broad coverage.

distractorExplanations.C: This delays necessary reassessment.
distractorExplanations.D: This does not address treatment failure.

distractorExplanations.C: This omits the IV antimicrobial treatment advised for suspected PID in pregnancy.

sections.title: Risk-based evaluation
sections.text: Current results, prior testing and treatment history determine risk; HPV16 or HPV18 warrants evaluation even with negative cytology.

sections.title: High-grade disease
sections.text: CIN3 is a direct precancer requiring treatment. Age, pregnancy and reproductive concerns alter other management pathways.

sections.title: Long-term surveillance
sections.text: After treatment and initial intensive surveillance for high-grade disease, HPV-based testing every three years continues for at least 25 years.

sections.title: Use screening and treatment history
sections.text: NCI explains that follow-up considers current screening results, previous results, prior treatment for precancer and age. A current result alone is not enough to assign one universal follow-up interval.

sections.title: Do not equate CIN 1 with invasive cancer
sections.text: NCI describes CIN 1 as mild, low-grade change that usually resolves and ordinarily does not require treatment. Follow-up still depends on the overall risk assessment; this is not permission to abandon surveillance.

sections.title: Secondary prevention depends on the available resource tier
sections.text: The ASCO 2022 update addresses cervical-cancer secondary prevention across four resource tiers. Its primary abstract distinguishes screening frequency, triage and treatment according to available resources. HPV testing is its recommended screening approach; abnormal triage in settings beyond Basic is followed by colposcopy. These selected abstract statements do not establish a complete individual-risk algorithm or a current United States screening schedule.

sections.title: Precancer treatment requires follow-up and eligibility
sections.text: The ASCO update’s abstract lists thermal ablation or loop electrosurgical excision for Basic settings, and excision or ablation for other settings, with a 12-month follow-up described across settings. Treatment eligibility and triage differ by tier. This abbreviated abstract summary does not provide lesion-size criteria, suspicion-of-invasion exclusions, pregnancy management or a full post-treatment surveillance schedule. Those missing details must not be inferred from this excerpt.

End screening immediately

One negative cytology permanently clears risk

questions.explanation: High-grade precancer treatment requires prolonged HPV-based surveillance.

Past screening results while omitting the precancer treatment history
Previous screening results, treatment history and age
HPV vaccination history as the sole follow-up determinant

distractorExplanations.B: The treatment-history difference in this vignette is part of the information the reference says to include.

questions.stem: Biopsy in an otherwise uncomplicated study case shows CIN 1. Which counseling statement best matches the NCI reference?

choices.text: It is a low-grade change that often resolves; arrange risk-appropriate follow-up
CIN 1 means that invasive cervical cancer has already been established
Immediate excision should be scheduled without considering the risk context
Manage the result as a high-grade CIN 3 lesion
Discontinue future screening because no immediate treatment is planned

questions.explanation: NCI describes CIN 1 as mild or low-grade change that usually resolves without treatment. The answer preserves follow-up and does not extrapolate to high-grade lesions or special populations.

distractorExplanations.B: NCI distinguishes this low-grade change from invasive cancer.
distractorExplanations.C: The reference describes frequent resolution of CIN 1 and a follow-up approach; it does not make immediate excision the default for this case.
distractorExplanations.D: This substitutes a different grade for the biopsy finding supplied.

sections.title: Screening window
sections.text: Screen asymptomatic pregnant persons without known diabetes at 24 weeks or later; routine earlier screening evidence is insufficient.

sections.title: Two-step testing
sections.text: In the common US two-step strategy, an abnormal glucose challenge leads to a diagnostic oral glucose tolerance test.

sections.title: Why detection matters
sections.text: Gestational diabetes increases maternal-fetal risks; treatment of screen-detected disease reduces outcomes such as macrosomia and shoulder dystocia.

sections.title: Escalate when lifestyle measures are insufficient
sections.text: The MedlinePlus summary describes healthy diet and regular physical activity to manage blood glucose during pregnancy, with diabetes medicines when these measures are insufficient. It does not specify a preferred drug, dose or glucose target.

sections.title: Follow the risk after delivery
sections.text: After gestational diabetes, test for type 2 diabetes within 4–12 weeks after birth. Even if glucose normalizes, repeat testing every 1–3 years. Resolution after pregnancy does not remove the later diabetes risk.

Exclude diabetes because she feels well
Screen for gestational diabetes now
Wait until delivery
Do not screen without symptoms

questions.explanation: USPSTF recommends screening from 24 weeks onward in this population.

distractorExplanations.B: Symptoms are not required for disease detection.
distractorExplanations.D: The recommended screening window is already reached.

Diagnose solely from the screening result
No further evaluation
Diagnostic oral glucose tolerance test
Repeat the same screen indefinitely

questions.explanation: The two-step pathway separates a screening challenge from the diagnostic tolerance test.

distractorExplanations.A: This is not the specified diagnostic step.
distractorExplanations.B: The two-step strategy requires confirmation.
distractorExplanations.C: The abnormal screen requires diagnostic follow-up.
distractorExplanations.E: The next step is diagnostic testing.

choices.text: Continue the same plan without reviewing treatment despite persistent above-target glucose
Replace glucose monitoring with monitoring symptoms alone
Further restrict nutrition while excluding medication from discussion
Discuss adding pregnancy-appropriate diabetes medication
Defer medication discussion until postpartum testing

distractorExplanations.A: The reference advises medication when diet and activity do not adequately manage glucose.
distractorExplanations.B: It does not address the documented failure to meet glucose targets.
distractorExplanations.C: The source supports adding medication when the agreed lifestyle measures are insufficient.
distractorExplanations.E: This leaves the persistent pregnancy glucose problem unaddressed.

questions.stem: Six weeks after delivery, a patient whose gestational diabetes appears to have resolved asks whether she still needs testing. What is the most appropriate plan?

choices.text: Test now, then stop testing unless another pregnancy occurs
Test now within the 4–12-week postpartum window, then every 1–3 years if normal
Omit postpartum testing if glucose appears normal
Wait one year for the first postpartum test
Wait for symptoms before ordering any further testing

questions.explanation: The government health-topic summary recommends testing within 4–12 weeks after birth and continued testing every 1–3 years even after normal glucose returns.

distractorExplanations.A: The reference also recommends continued testing every 1–3 years.
distractorExplanations.C: Apparent resolution does not remove the recommended postpartum testing.
distractorExplanations.D: The first recommended window is 4–12 weeks after delivery.
distractorExplanations.E: The reference describes scheduled testing rather than symptom-triggered testing alone.

questions.learningObjective: Plan postpartum and ongoing diabetes screening after gestational diabetes.

sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: New hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or specified organ dysfunction supports preeclampsia; proteinuria is not obligatory when qualifying organ findings occur.

sections.title: Antenatal detection
sections.text: Measure blood pressure throughout pregnancy, including each prenatal visit, to detect hypertensive disorders that may be clinically silent.

sections.title: High-risk history
sections.text: Prior preeclampsia, multifetal gestation, chronic hypertension, pregestational diabetes, kidney disease or specified autoimmune disease confer high risk.

sections.title: Risk-based prevention
sections.text: For eligible high-risk asymptomatic pregnancy, low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily after 12 weeks is recommended; assess contraindications.

sections.title: Disease may begin after delivery
sections.text: Postpartum preeclampsia can develop even without antenatal hypertension or preeclampsia. NICHD describes onset usually from 48 hours to 6 weeks after birth, with possible severe headache, visual symptoms, upper abdominal pain and hypertension. Prompt recognition matters.

sections.title: Interpret the HELLP combination
sections.text: HELLP describes hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets, associated with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. These findings indicate a serious complication; they are not explained away solely by a resolved delivery.

choices.text: Wait until severe hypertension develops
Aspirin only once at delivery
No prophylaxis because she is asymptomatic
A routine antibiotic course
Low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily

questions.explanation: Chronic hypertension is a high-risk factor supporting low-dose aspirin after 12 weeks.

distractorExplanations.A: Prophylaxis precedes clinical disease.
distractorExplanations.B: The preventive regimen is daily.
distractorExplanations.C: Prevention targets asymptomatic high-risk pregnancy.
distractorExplanations.D: Antibiotics do not provide this prophylaxis.

questions.learningObjective: Identify aspirin prophylaxis for a high-risk pregnancy.

choices.text: Chronic hypertension predating pregnancy
Gestational hypertension without preeclampsia
Gestational diabetes
Preeclampsia

questions.explanation: New hypertension after 20 weeks accompanied by proteinuria supports preeclampsia.

distractorExplanations.A: She was previously normotensive.
distractorExplanations.B: Proteinuria supports preeclampsia rather than isolated hypertension.
distractorExplanations.C: Glucose abnormalities are not described.
distractorExplanations.E: No seizures are reported.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the hypertension-plus-proteinuria presentation of preeclampsia.

questions.stem: Ten days after an uncomplicated pregnancy, a patient develops hypertension, a severe headache and visual changes. Which postpartum hypertensive complication must be assessed promptly despite normal antenatal blood pressure?

choices.text: Primary hypertension
Migraine
Post-dural-puncture headache
Expected postpartum fluid shifts
Postpartum preeclampsia

questions.explanation: NICHD describes postpartum preeclampsia even after a normotensive pregnancy and lists severe headache, visual changes and hypertension among possible symptoms. The presentation warrants prompt evaluation in the study scenario.

distractorExplanations.A: NICHD identifies this postpartum symptom combination as a presentation in which preeclampsia remains a concern.
distractorExplanations.B: It does not address the hypertensive postpartum pattern emphasized in the reference.
distractorExplanations.C: That attribution does not replace assessment of the postpartum hypertensive syndrome supplied.
distractorExplanations.D: It overlooks the headache and visual symptoms identified by NICHD as possible warning features.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize postpartum preeclampsia without requiring prior antenatal hypertension.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient with a hypertensive disorder has hemolysis, rising liver enzymes and a low platelet count. Which named obstetric complication is defined by this triad?

choices.text: Gestational hypertension without an organ-related complication
Isolated iron-deficiency anemia
HELLP syndrome
Isolated gestational thrombocytopenia
Eclampsia defined solely by this laboratory triad

questions.explanation: NICHD defines HELLP by hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets. The question asks syndrome recognition, not a laboratory cutoff, magnesium regimen or delivery-timing rule.

distractorExplanations.A: It does not account for the defining laboratory triad in the question.
distractorExplanations.B: It does not match the named complication defined by the three supplied findings.
distractorExplanations.D: It does not integrate hemolysis and elevated liver enzymes with the platelet abnormality.
distractorExplanations.E: NICHD names HELLP, rather than eclampsia, for the supplied triad.

sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: Ectopic pregnancy lies outside the uterine cavity, most often in a fallopian tube.

sections.title: Unstable presentation
sections.text: Hemodynamic instability with tubal ectopic pregnancy is an emergency requiring prompt surgical intervention.

sections.title: Selected stable treatment
sections.text: Early stable tubal ectopic pregnancy may be managed with minimally invasive surgery or methotrexate after specialist eligibility assessment.

sections.title: A positive pregnancy test does not establish location
sections.text: The MedlinePlus summary describes blood testing and ultrasound in diagnosing ectopic pregnancy. A pregnancy test confirms pregnancy; it does not alone demonstrate that the pregnancy is inside the uterus. This reference supplies no discriminatory hCG threshold.

sections.title: Maintain suspicion in a symptomatic pregnancy
sections.text: Prior PID, ectopic pregnancy and pelvic or tubal surgery increase ectopic risk. Becoming pregnant with an IUD is also a risk context. Early ectopic symptoms can include pelvic pain and light vaginal bleeding; the source does not quantify absolute IUD-associated risk.

questions.stem: A patient with confirmed tubal ectopic pregnancy develops hypotension and altered mentation. Which treatment priority is appropriate?

choices.text: Expectant outpatient observation
Prompt emergency surgical intervention with stabilization
Routine outpatient methotrexate
Repeat testing in one week
Oral contraception alone

questions.explanation: An unstable tubal ectopic pregnancy requires prompt surgical management.

distractorExplanations.A: Instability precludes this approach.
distractorExplanations.C: Instability requires emergency surgery.
distractorExplanations.D: Delay is inappropriate in an unstable emergency.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not treat the ectopic emergency.

An oral antibiotic
A combined contraceptive pill

distractorExplanations.A: It does not treat ectopic pregnancy.
distractorExplanations.B: It has no role in this treatment.
distractorExplanations.D: It is not the cited ectopic treatment.
distractorExplanations.E: It is not medical treatment of established ectopic pregnancy.

questions.learningObjective: Identify medical therapy after ectopic treatment eligibility assessment.

questions.stem: A patient has a positive pregnancy test, pelvic pain and light vaginal bleeding. She is stable, and no ultrasound has been obtained. What additional diagnostic approach addresses the pregnancy-location concern?

choices.text: Blood testing together with pelvic ultrasound
Repeat urine pregnancy testing as the only next investigation
Serial pregnancy blood testing while omitting pelvic imaging
A pelvic examination as the only location assessment
Routine prenatal follow-up without evaluating the current pain and bleeding

questions.explanation: MedlinePlus describes blood tests and ultrasound for ectopic diagnosis. No hCG threshold, serial-testing schedule or methotrexate eligibility criterion is inferred from this reference.

distractorExplanations.B: It does not address the location concern with the blood-testing and ultrasound approach described by the reference.
distractorExplanations.C: The cited diagnostic approach includes ultrasound as well as blood tests.
distractorExplanations.D: It omits the blood-testing and ultrasound approach described for this concern.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not address the current ectopic-pregnancy concern in this vignette.

questions.learningObjective: Choose a diagnostic approach that evaluates location rather than pregnancy status alone.

questions.stem: An adult with a prior PID history now has a positive pregnancy test, pelvic pain and light vaginal bleeding. Which prior-history interpretation is most appropriate?

choices.text: Prior PID is relevant only if infection symptoms are still present
The PID history lowers concern for an ectopic pregnancy
Prior PID affects fertility but has no relevance once a pregnancy test is positive
Prior PID increases concern for ectopic pregnancy
Prior PID establishes the ectopic diagnosis without location assessment

questions.explanation: The government summary lists prior PID among ectopic risk factors and pelvic pain with light bleeding among possible early symptoms. Risk supports assessment; it does not prove the diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.A: The reference lists a history of PID as a risk factor, without requiring current infection symptoms.
distractorExplanations.B: That reverses the risk direction reported in the government summary.
distractorExplanations.C: The reference identifies prior PID as relevant to ectopic-pregnancy risk.
distractorExplanations.E: A listed risk factor supports concern but does not establish the pregnancy location.

questions.learningObjective: Apply a tubal-injury risk factor without turning risk into a diagnosis.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text: Compatible vaginitis plus yeast on microscopy or testing supports candidiasis; vaginal pH is usually normal, below 4.5.

sections.title: Pregnancy treatment
sections.text: Pregnancy calls for a seven-day topical azole course; oral fluconazole should not be used.

sections.title: Complicated presentations
sections.text: Persistent or recurrent symptoms warrant evaluation, with culture or PCR in complicated disease to identify non-albicans species.

sections.title: Do not treat a culture result alone
sections.text: Candida detected by vaginal culture without signs or symptoms is not by itself an indication for treatment. Colonization occurs in some otherwise healthy women.

sections.title: Negative microscopy can need culture
sections.text: For persistent signs or symptoms consistent with candidiasis and a negative wet mount, CDC advises considering vaginal Candida culture. If culture cannot be performed, empiric treatment can be considered; negative microscopy alone does not settle the diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.C: A different antifungal route does not change the absence of a treatment indication in this asymptomatic case.
distractorExplanations.D: The current culture result alone does not establish symptomatic disease needing treatment.

distractorExplanations.B: It does not provide the organism confirmation requested; CDC describes culture for this situation.
distractorExplanations.C: That is not the diagnostic next step described by CDC for this presentation.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text: Three Amsel findings support BV: homogeneous discharge, clue cells, pH above 4.5 and amine odor are the four criteria.

sections.title: Initial symptomatic treatment
sections.text: Oral metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for seven days is one recommended regimen; vaginal alternatives also exist.

sections.title: Symptomatic pregnancy
sections.text: Treat symptomatic BV in pregnancy. This record does not address updated partner therapy for recurrent BV.

sections.title: Use appropriate diagnostic tests
sections.text: CDC describes BV NAATs for symptomatic women because accuracy is not well defined without symptoms. Pap testing has no clinical utility for BV diagnosis, and Gardnerella culture is not recommended because it lacks specificity. Amsel criteria and vaginal Gram stain remain useful.

sections.title: Distinguish oral intolerance from allergy
sections.text: Intravaginal metronidazole gel can be considered when a patient is not allergic to metronidazole but cannot tolerate the oral formulation. This does not apply to an actual metronidazole allergy.

Acyclovir
Doxycycline alone

distractorExplanations.A: Symptomatic BV warrants treatment.
distractorExplanations.C: This targets yeast rather than BV.

Use Gardnerella culture as the specific diagnostic standard
Use a BV diagnostic method such as Amsel criteria, vaginal Gram stain or an appropriate NAAT
Diagnose BV from odor alone without completing a validated assessment
Use an incomplete Amsel assessment as if all required criteria were met

Substitute a metronidazole skin product for an intravaginal formulation
Choose oral tinidazole as the local metronidazole formulation
Use an IV route as the routine alternative for this uncomplicated case

sections.title: Testing
sections.text: Wet-mount sensitivity is limited; a negative result does not exclude trichomoniasis, and available molecular testing improves detection.

sections.title: Treatment
sections.text: For women, oral metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for seven days is recommended; the male regimen differs.

sections.title: Reinfection prevention
sections.text: Treat current partners, abstain until treatment and symptoms resolve, and retest sexually active women at about three months.

sections.title: Follow a negative wet mount when suspicion persists
sections.text: Wet-mount sensitivity for trichomoniasis is limited. When available, a more sensitive molecular diagnostic test should accompany a negative wet mount in a patient whose evaluation still suggests infection.

sections.title: Avoid premature NAAT interpretation
sections.text: For persistent or recurrent trichomoniasis, culture is the preferred retest. If NAAT is used, wait at least 3 weeks after treatment completion because residual nucleic acid can cause a clinically misleading result. Assess adherence and reexposure as well.

questions.stem: A woman has NAAT-confirmed trichomoniasis and no treatment contraindication. Which CDC regimen is recommended?

choices.text: Acyclovir for seven days
No treatment after a positive NAAT
Metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for seven days
Vaginal metronidazole gel alone
Fluconazole once

questions.explanation: Women receive the seven-day oral metronidazole regimen.

distractorExplanations.A: It is not trichomoniasis treatment.
distractorExplanations.B: Confirmed infection warrants treatment.
distractorExplanations.D: The gel is not recommended for trichomoniasis.
distractorExplanations.E: It treats yeast, not trichomoniasis.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish recommended oral treatment from inappropriate local therapy.

questions.stem: A sexually active woman completed trichomoniasis treatment and believes her partner was treated. What follow-up is still recommended?

choices.text: Only repeat a wet mount immediately
Routine lifelong monthly testing
Use a Pap smear as the follow-up infection test
Retesting for trichomoniasis at about three months
No retesting because the partner was treated

questions.explanation: CDC recommends approximately three-month retesting regardless of presumed partner treatment.

distractorExplanations.A: This does not replace the recommended later retest.
distractorExplanations.B: That schedule is not recommended here.
distractorExplanations.C: A dedicated infection test is appropriate.
distractorExplanations.E: Reinfection risk still warrants retesting.

questions.learningObjective: Apply recommended retesting after treated trichomoniasis.

questions.stem: A woman with vaginal discharge has a negative wet mount, but trichomoniasis remains a concern. A validated molecular test is available. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

choices.text: Repeat wet mounts alone rather than use the available molecular test
Treat a partner’s diagnosis as confirmation of the patient’s infection
Use incidental cervical cytology as a definitive trichomonas test
Obtain an appropriate trichomonas NAAT
Assign the diagnosis from discharge symptoms alone

questions.explanation: CDC recommends sensitive molecular diagnostic options with a negative wet mount when possible. This is a diagnostic next-step item, distinct from selecting the treatment regimen or later routine reinfection screening.

distractorExplanations.A: The reference recommends a more sensitive molecular option when the wet mount is negative and testing is available.
distractorExplanations.B: It does not establish the patient’s infection with the diagnostic next step requested.
distractorExplanations.C: CDC does not treat a Pap result as definitive confirmation of trichomoniasis.
distractorExplanations.E: The available molecular test addresses the remaining diagnostic uncertainty.

questions.learningObjective: Use a sensitive test when wet-mount microscopy does not resolve suspected trichomoniasis.

questions.stem: One week after completing trichomoniasis treatment, a patient still has symptoms. NAAT is being considered to evaluate possible persistent infection. Which testing principle is most appropriate?

choices.text: Use a NAAT immediately as definitive proof of viable persistent infection
Do not perform NAAT before 3 weeks after treatment completion
Wait one more week and perform NAAT at two weeks after completion
Avoid NAAT permanently after any trichomoniasis treatment
Defer all clinical assessment until the routine three-month retest

questions.explanation: CDC prefers culture for persistent or recurrent infection and cautions against NAAT before 3 weeks after completion because it may detect residual nucleic acid. This waiting rule applies to NAAT, not to all clinical assessment.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC warns that an early NAAT may detect residual nucleic acid.
distractorExplanations.C: This is still before the 3-week minimum described for this use of NAAT.
distractorExplanations.D: The CDC restriction concerns testing before 3 weeks, rather than a permanent prohibition.
distractorExplanations.E: The NAAT timing rule does not require delaying clinical assessment of persistent symptoms.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish persistent-infection NAAT timing from routine reinfection screening.

sections.title: Early syphilis treatment
sections.text: For nonpregnant adults with primary or secondary syphilis, benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once is recommended.

sections.title: Pregnancy and allergy
sections.text: No proven nonpenicillin alternative prevents congenital infection; confirmed allergy in pregnancy requires desensitization and stage-appropriate penicillin.

sections.title: Follow-up
sections.text: Early syphilis requires clinical and quantitative serologic follow-up; staging and neurologic findings affect evaluation and treatment.

sections.title: Neurologic findings change evaluation
sections.text: CDC advises evaluation including CSF analysis for syphilis with neurologic signs such as cranial nerve dysfunction, meningitis, stroke or altered mental state. Routine CSF analysis is not recommended for uncomplicated primary or secondary syphilis without clinical neurologic or ophthalmic findings.

sections.title: Follow response with comparable nontreponemal titers
sections.text: Treponemal tests often stay reactive after adequate treatment and their titers do not measure treatment response. Compare quantitative nontreponemal results using the same method, preferably the same laboratory; RPR and VDRL values are not directly interchangeable.

questions.stem: A nonpregnant adult has confirmed primary syphilis without neurologic or ocular findings. Which regimen is recommended?

choices.text: Oral amoxicillin as the standard regimen
Topical antibiotic to the chancre alone
No treatment because the lesion may heal
An antifungal course
Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once

questions.explanation: The recommended adult primary/secondary regimen is a single benzathine penicillin G dose.

distractorExplanations.A: It is not the recommended standard regimen.
distractorExplanations.B: Local treatment does not address systemic infection.
distractorExplanations.C: Lesion healing does not eliminate infection.
distractorExplanations.D: It does not treat syphilis.

questions.learningObjective: Identify standard treatment for uncomplicated primary syphilis.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient has syphilis and confirmed immediate penicillin allergy. Which plan best follows CDC guidance?

choices.text: Desensitization followed by stage-appropriate penicillin G
Substitute doxycycline as equally proven fetal protection
Defer all treatment until delivery
Use topical treatment alone
Treat only the partner

questions.explanation: Penicillin is required in pregnancy; allergy is managed through desensitization.

distractorExplanations.B: No proven penicillin alternative exists in pregnancy.
distractorExplanations.C: This leaves maternal and fetal infection untreated.
distractorExplanations.D: It cannot treat systemic infection.
distractorExplanations.E: The pregnant patient also requires treatment.

questions.learningObjective: Manage penicillin allergy when treating syphilis during pregnancy.

questions.stem: A patient with confirmed early syphilis develops a new cranial nerve abnormality. Which evaluation is appropriate beyond routine uncomplicated early-syphilis management?

choices.text: Obtain a serum nontreponemal titer as the only neurologic assessment
Use HIV testing alone to assess the cranial nerve finding
Repeat a serum treponemal test to exclude nervous-system involvement
Wait for routine follow-up to see whether the nerve finding resolves
Neurologic evaluation including CSF analysis

questions.explanation: CDC recommends evaluation including CSF analysis when clinical neurologic signs such as cranial nerve dysfunction are present. This is different from routine CSF testing in uncomplicated asymptomatic early disease.

distractorExplanations.A: The new neurologic sign meets the CDC context for evaluation including CSF analysis.
distractorExplanations.B: It does not replace the neurologic evaluation described for this sign.
distractorExplanations.C: That does not provide the CSF assessment indicated by the clinical neurologic sign.
distractorExplanations.D: The reference supports current neurologic evaluation rather than deferral for this presentation.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the neurologic indication for additional syphilis evaluation.

questions.stem: After adequate syphilis treatment, a patient remains treponemal-test positive. Which method best assesses serologic treatment response?

choices.text: Require the treponemal test to become negative before considering response
Compare an RPR titer directly with a VDRL titer
Compare quantitative nontreponemal titers using the same testing method
Use the treponemal antibody titer alone to assess treatment response
Compare only qualitative reactive or nonreactive nontreponemal results

questions.explanation: CDC describes comparable quantitative nontreponemal titers for response assessment and warns that treponemal tests may remain reactive. Clinical findings and exposure history also matter.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC notes that treponemal reactivity may persist despite treatment.
distractorExplanations.B: CDC advises consistent methods for comparable nontreponemal titers.
distractorExplanations.D: The reference describes quantitative nontreponemal titers for this purpose.
distractorExplanations.E: This omits the quantitative titer comparison described for assessing response.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret persistent treponemal positivity without mistaking it for treatment failure.

sections.title: First episode
sections.text: Treat every first clinical genital herpes episode with systemic antiviral therapy; topical antivirals provide little benefit.

sections.title: Recurrent disease
sections.text: Daily suppressive antivirals reduce HSV-2 recurrences and can reduce transmission in appropriate symptomatic discordant couples.

sections.title: Counseling
sections.text: Treatment does not eradicate latent virus. Condoms and avoiding sex during outbreaks complement suppression; shedding can occur without lesions.

sections.title: Use the lesion when it is present
sections.text: Active genital lesions should be tested with type-specific NAAT or culture to confirm suspected herpes. NAAT is the most sensitive lesion test; blood PCR and blind swabs without a lesion are not routine tests for localized genital herpes.

sections.title: Confirm a low-positive HSV-2 EIA
sections.text: Commercial HSV-2 EIAs, especially low index values below 3.0, can be falsely positive. CDC advises a different confirmatory method such as Biokit or Western blot before interpretation. HSV IgM is not recommended.

questions.stem: A patient has a first clinical episode of laboratory-confirmed genital herpes. Lesions are mild and she can take oral medication. Which plan is appropriate?

choices.text: Antibiotics alone
Systemic oral antiviral therapy
Topical antiviral alone
No treatment because lesions are mild
An oral antifungal

questions.explanation: Even mild first episodes warrant systemic antiviral treatment.

distractorExplanations.A: No bacterial infection is identified.
distractorExplanations.C: Topical treatment offers minimal benefit.
distractorExplanations.D: All first episodes should receive antivirals.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not treat HSV.

questions.learningObjective: Treat a first genital herpes episode appropriately.

questions.stem: A patient with frequent symptomatic HSV-2 recurrences wants to reduce outbreaks and transmission to a susceptible partner. Which strategy best fits?

choices.text: Use antibiotics indefinitely
Tell the couple condoms are unnecessary
Daily suppression plus transmission-risk counseling
Promise that suppression eradicates HSV
Avoid sex only when fever occurs

questions.explanation: Suppressive antivirals reduce recurrence and can reduce, rather than eliminate, transmission risk.

distractorExplanations.A: Antibiotics do not suppress HSV.
distractorExplanations.B: Barrier counseling remains part of prevention.
distractorExplanations.D: Latent infection is not eradicated.
distractorExplanations.E: Outbreaks and asymptomatic shedding remain relevant.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the benefits and limits of HSV-2 suppression.

questions.stem: An adult presents with a fresh genital vesicle and no evidence of disseminated infection. Which test most directly confirms and types suspected localized genital herpes?

choices.text: Type-specific HSV NAAT from the lesion
Blood HSV PCR as the routine localized-genital test
A blind swab from normal skin instead of the fresh lesion
HSV IgM as the preferred confirmation test
Type-specific antibody testing instead of sampling the fresh lesion

questions.explanation: CDC recommends virologic testing from genital lesions, with NAAT the most sensitive option. The stem excludes suspected dissemination, where the role of blood testing differs.

distractorExplanations.B: CDC directs lesion testing for this localized presentation; the blood-PCR context differs.
distractorExplanations.C: It does not use the available lesion for the direct virologic confirmation described.
distractorExplanations.D: CDC does not recommend HSV IgM for this purpose.
distractorExplanations.E: Serology has other uses, but lesion NAAT directly addresses the fresh localized lesion in this question.

questions.learningObjective: Select lesion-based virologic confirmation for localized genital herpes.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic adult has an HSV-2 EIA index of 1.6. Before interpreting this as a definitive infection diagnosis, what is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Accept the single low-positive EIA as a definitive diagnosis
Use HSV IgM as the confirmation
Use an immunoblot based on the same antigen as the EIA
Obtain confirmation with a different method such as Biokit or Western blot
Repeat the same EIA and treat repeated low-positive results as independent confirmation

questions.explanation: CDC advises confirmation of low-index HSV-2 EIA results with a second method before interpretation because specificity is limited. This does not create a recommendation for routine asymptomatic population screening.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC highlights limited specificity at low index values and recommends confirmation.
distractorExplanations.B: CDC does not recommend HSV IgM for confirming this result.
distractorExplanations.C: The reference calls for a different confirmatory method rather than this same-antigen approach.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not provide the different-method confirmation recommended before interpretation.

questions.learningObjective: Confirm a low-positive HSV-2 antibody result before labeling infection.

sections.title: Evaluation across settings
sections.text: Document developmentally inappropriate, impairing symptoms across settings using caregiver and school reports; consider mimics and coexisting conditions.

sections.title: Preschool treatment
sections.text: Parent training in behavior management is initial treatment in preschool children; medication is considered for persistent serious impairment.

sections.title: School-age treatment
sections.text: For school-age children, FDA-approved medication combines with parent/classroom behavioral strategies and educational supports.

sections.title: Combine medication and behavioral supports
sections.text: For children age 6 years and older, CDC summarizes treatment using FDA-approved medication with parent behavior-management training and/or available classroom interventions. Educational and individual school supports are part of the plan.

sections.title: Escalate selected preschool cases after behavior intervention
sections.text: For preschool children, methylphenidate may be used if behavioral intervention does not produce significant improvement and serious problems persist. This is a conditional escalation after behavioral treatment, not routine medication before trying it.

sections.title: Typical presentation
sections.text: An infant with a first viral wheezing illness and diffuse findings is usually diagnosed clinically; routine imaging and laboratory testing are unnecessary.

sections.title: Supportive management
sections.text: For uncomplicated infant bronchiolitis, prioritize respiratory and hydration assessment; routine albuterol, steroids and antibiotics are not recommended.

sections.title: Feeding difficulty
sections.text: Infants unable to maintain intake need consideration of nasogastric or intravenous hydration according to respiratory status and clinical judgment.

sections.title: Investigate an atypical deterioration selectively
sections.text: In the 2025 Australasian guideline, routine chest radiography is discouraged conditionally. Considering a radiograph for unexpected deterioration or a course inconsistent with bronchiolitis is consensus-based, particularly when a complication such as pneumothorax or pneumonia is suspected. These are international recommendations, not an asserted US board rule.

sections.title: Discharge readiness includes the home setting
sections.text: The international guideline considers clinical stability, feeding, oxygen-support needs, caregiver ability to manage at home, education about deterioration, transport access and local follow-up. Apparent clinical improvement alone does not address every discharge-readiness factor.

Antibiotics without bacterial evidence

distractorExplanations.C: No concomitant bacterial infection is described.

distractorExplanations.E: It is not routine recommended care.

distractorExplanations.E: Feeding safety must be assessed.

questions.learningObjective: Provide hydration support when infant oral intake is inadequate.

questions.stem: An infant hospitalized with bronchiolitis unexpectedly deteriorates, with concern for pneumothorax or another complication. Under the cited international guideline, what diagnostic action may be considered?

choices.text: Repeat a respiratory viral swab as the only assessment of the suspected pneumothorax
Use an improving infant’s routine chest-radiograph policy instead of reassessing this deterioration
A chest radiograph directed at the suspected complication
Treat the original bronchiolitis diagnosis as sufficient and defer reassessment
Order a blood culture alone to assess the suspected pneumothorax

questions.explanation: The 2025 Australasian guideline has a consensus-based recommendation to consider CXR for unexpected deterioration or an atypical course. This is distinguished from its conditional recommendation against routine CXR.

distractorExplanations.A: It does not address the suspected structural complication for which the guideline allows directed imaging.
distractorExplanations.B: The guideline distinguishes routine imaging from imaging considered for unexpected deterioration.
distractorExplanations.D: The supplied change in course is the situation in which the guideline supports considering further investigation.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not provide the directed imaging assessment of the suspected complication.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a selective imaging indication while preserving the international scope and recommendation strength.

questions.stem: An infant with bronchiolitis has improved clinically, but the caregiver is unsure how to recognize deterioration and has no arranged follow-up or reliable transport. Which step addresses discharge readiness in the cited guideline?

choices.text: Resolve caregiver education, transport and follow-up concerns before finalizing discharge
Finalize discharge from the improved examination alone
Arrange a routine chest radiograph instead of resolving the practical discharge concerns
Defer caregiver education until the next clinical visit
Use a fixed observation interval as a substitute for checking access to care

questions.explanation: The Australasian guideline includes caregiver capacity, return advice, transport and local follow-up alongside clinical stability, feeding and support requirements. This question does not impose an unsupported fixed admission duration.

distractorExplanations.B: It omits caregiver capacity, transport and follow-up considerations in the guideline.
distractorExplanations.C: Routine imaging does not resolve the discharge-readiness concerns specified.
distractorExplanations.D: The guideline includes caregiver readiness and return advice in the discharge assessment.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not address the caregiver, transport and follow-up concerns described in the guideline.

questions.learningObjective: Integrate caregiver readiness and access into bronchiolitis discharge planning.

sections.title: Recognition and severity
sections.text: Barky cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor suggest croup; stridor at rest and increased work of breathing indicate greater severity.

sections.title: Initial therapy
sections.text: Dexamethasone is used across typical croup severity levels; nebulized epinephrine treats clinically significant stridor and respiratory distress.

sections.title: Reassessment and disposition
sections.text: Persistent stridor at rest or substantial work of breathing after treatment supports admission; discharge depends on sustained clinical improvement.

sections.title: A typical presentation is a clinical diagnosis
sections.text: The cited clinical review describes viral croup as a clinical diagnosis: barking cough, hoarseness and stridor after upper-respiratory symptoms. Most typical cases do not need extra tests merely to confirm croup. Atypical or concerning presentations require a different assessment.

sections.title: An acute adjunct for substantial upper-airway obstruction
sections.text: The review describes nebulized epinephrine for moderate-to-severe upper-airway obstruction with increased breathing difficulty. It is an acute adjunct to corticosteroid treatment; this source does not establish a drug dose or a universal observation/discharge interval for this app.

questions.stem: A well-appearing 2-year-old has a barky cough and hoarse voice but no stridor at rest or significant distress. Which medication is recommended for typical croup?

choices.text: No steroid because the illness is mild
Daily repeat dexamethasone automatically
A single dexamethasone dose
Routine antibiotics
Albuterol as the main croup treatment

questions.explanation: Typical mild croup still benefits from a single dexamethasone treatment.

distractorExplanations.A: Dexamethasone is recommended across severity levels.
distractorExplanations.B: Routine repeated steroid dosing is not recommended.
distractorExplanations.D: No bacterial alternative diagnosis is described.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not target typical upper-airway disease.

questions.learningObjective: Use steroid therapy in typical mild croup.

questions.stem: A child with croup still has stridor at rest and moderate work of breathing after dexamethasone and nebulized epinephrine. What disposition is supported?

choices.text: Discharge because epinephrine was given once
Routine follow-up in a month
Replace monitoring with empiric oral antibiotics
Hospital admission for continued monitoring and treatment
Immediate discharge without reassessment

questions.explanation: Persistent stridor and respiratory work despite treatment are admission criteria.

distractorExplanations.A: Disposition depends on response, not simply treatment receipt.
distractorExplanations.B: Ongoing respiratory distress needs current assessment.
distractorExplanations.C: No bacterial diagnosis is established.
distractorExplanations.E: Persistent moderate symptoms support admission.

questions.learningObjective: Base croup disposition on persistent symptoms after therapy.

questions.stem: A well-appearing 2-year-old has a typical barking cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor after coryza. There are no atypical findings. Which diagnostic approach best fits the cited review?

choices.text: Obtain routine neck radiographs to confirm every typical presentation
Obtain viral typing before making the clinical diagnosis
Arrange bronchoscopy as the routine first confirmation test
Make a clinical diagnosis without routine additional tests solely to confirm croup
Obtain a CBC as a required confirmation test

questions.explanation: The peer-reviewed review describes a typical croup presentation as a clinical diagnosis without routine additional confirmation testing. The answer does not apply to atypical features or suspected alternative diagnoses.

distractorExplanations.A: The review describes a clinical diagnosis without routine additional confirmation testing in typical cases.
distractorExplanations.B: The typical clinical approach described does not require viral confirmation first.
distractorExplanations.C: The review does not make invasive confirmation routine for this typical presentation.
distractorExplanations.E: The reference describes typical croup as a clinical diagnosis without routine confirmation testing.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid unnecessary confirmation testing in a typical croup presentation.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with croup has stridor at rest and substantial upper-airway obstruction with increased work of breathing. Corticosteroid treatment has been given. Which acute adjunct is described for moderate-to-severe obstruction?

choices.text: Start antibiotics before addressing the obstruction because the cough is barky
Nebulized epinephrine
Use an inhaled lower-airway bronchodilator as the sole acute adjunct
Use a routine second corticosteroid dose as the only immediate adjunct
Use supplemental oxygen alone as the entire additional response to stridor

questions.explanation: The cited clinical review supports nebulized epinephrine for moderate-to-severe upper-airway obstruction. This item adds neither a dose nor a fixed observation interval, and does not replace clinical monitoring.

distractorExplanations.A: The scenario supplies typical croup rather than a bacterial alternative; the review names an acute adjunct for substantial obstruction.
distractorExplanations.C: It is not the nebulized epinephrine adjunct identified by this review for the upper-airway presentation.
distractorExplanations.D: The review identifies nebulized epinephrine for substantial obstruction and does not establish routine multiple steroid doses as the acute adjunct.
distractorExplanations.E: The review includes nebulized epinephrine for this degree of upper-airway obstruction; supportive measures do not replace that selection.

questions.learningObjective: Select the acute adjunct for moderate-to-severe croup obstruction.

limitations: US institutional consensus. The 2026 page has inconsistent fixed epinephrine-dose disposition thresholds; this module excludes that issue and uses persistent clinical symptoms.

sections.title: Collection quality
sections.text: For a non-toilet-trained child needing definitive culture, catheter collection is preferred over a bag specimen prone to contamination.

sections.title: Interpretation
sections.text: Interpret pyuria and culture together with symptoms and collection method; negative nitrite alone does not exclude infection.

sections.title: Selective imaging
sections.text: VCUG is not routine after a first febrile UTI; concerning ultrasound findings or selected recurrent infections can justify it.

sections.title: Consider hospital and IV treatment when oral therapy is not feasible
sections.text: NIDDK describes oral antibiotics for many children older than 2 months, with possible hospital IV treatment for younger infants or children who are vomiting. Antibiotic selection depends on age, organism and allergies; this reference gives no empirical drug or treatment-duration rule.

sections.title: Address bowel and bladder factors
sections.text: For preventing recurrent bladder infection, NIDDK advises adequate fluids, responding to the urge to urinate, complete bladder emptying and avoiding constipation. Related problems such as constipation may need treatment. These preventive measures do not replace treatment of a bacterial infection.

questions.stem: A febrile 10-month-old needs a reliable urine culture. A bag urinalysis screen is positive and catheterization is feasible. What is the preferred next specimen?

choices.text: Culture the bag specimen as equally reliable
Culture stool instead
Use fever alone as culture confirmation
Ignore the positive screen
Catheter-obtained urine for culture

questions.explanation: A positive bag screen should lead to a more reliable catheter culture when feasible.

distractorExplanations.A: Bag contamination limits definitive culture interpretation.
distractorExplanations.B: It does not establish urinary infection.
distractorExplanations.C: A reliable urine specimen is needed.
distractorExplanations.D: Further diagnostic collection is warranted.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish screening urine from definitive culture collection.

questions.stem: A child recovered from a first febrile UTI. Renal ultrasound is reassuring, with no obstruction concerns or recurrent infection. What is the role of VCUG?

choices.text: It is not routinely indicated
Required for every first febrile UTI
Required daily until the urine is sterile
Replaces urine culture for diagnosis
Never indicated even with future obstruction concerns

questions.explanation: First infection alone with reassuring imaging does not require routine VCUG.

distractorExplanations.B: The guideline reserves VCUG for selected indications.
distractorExplanations.C: This is not a recommended imaging schedule.
distractorExplanations.D: Imaging does not replace microbiologic diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.E: Selected concerning findings can warrant VCUG.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid routine VCUG after an uncomplicated first febrile UTI.

questions.stem: A 7-month-old with a confirmed bacterial UTI is repeatedly vomiting and cannot retain oral antibiotic doses. What is the most appropriate general next consideration?

choices.text: Continue the same outpatient oral plan without reassessing repeated vomiting
Change to another oral formulation without addressing the inability to retain liquids
Defer antibiotics until vomiting resolves without reassessing the setting
Monitor hydration alone while postponing infection treatment
Evaluate for hospital-based IV antibiotic treatment

questions.explanation: NIDDK describes possible hospital IV antibiotics for children who are vomiting. The scenario asks for a route and setting reassessment, not an automatic hospitalization rule for every child with a UTI.

distractorExplanations.A: It does not address the ongoing inability to retain the prescribed doses.
distractorExplanations.B: The route problem remains, and NIDDK describes possible hospital IV treatment for vomiting children.
distractorExplanations.C: It leaves the confirmed infection and inability to take treatment unresolved.
distractorExplanations.D: NIDDK describes antibiotic treatment and a possible IV setting in this vomiting context.

questions.learningObjective: Adapt pediatric UTI treatment when the oral route is not feasible.

questions.stem: A toilet-trained child has recurrent bladder infections and chronic constipation. Current infection treatment is complete. Which preventive counseling is most appropriate?

choices.text: Encourage longer intervals between voids to reduce bathroom visits
Restrict fluids solely to reduce urinary frequency
Treat constipation and support regular, complete bladder emptying
Address bowel habits but leave incomplete or postponed bladder emptying unaddressed
Focus only on external hygiene while leaving chronic constipation untreated

questions.explanation: NIDDK includes constipation treatment and healthy voiding habits in preventing childhood bladder infections. This is general government clinical education, not an AAP antibiotic or imaging guideline.

distractorExplanations.A: It does not follow the regular bladder-emptying habits described by NIDDK.
distractorExplanations.B: It does not match the healthy fluid and voiding measures described in the reference.
distractorExplanations.D: The cited prevention approach includes both constipation care and healthy voiding habits.
distractorExplanations.E: It omits the constipation concern explicitly included in NIDDK prevention counseling.

questions.learningObjective: Address modifiable bowel and bladder contributors to recurrent pediatric UTI.

limitations: US institutional consensus, not the retired AAP 2011 UTI algorithm. Antibiotic choice and duration must reflect the current local stewardship guidance.

sections.title: Confirm and investigate
sections.text: Document iron deficiency and consider gastrointestinal causes when anemia has no obvious explanation; replacement alone does not identify occult bleeding.

sections.title: Adult endoscopic evaluation
sections.text: AGA recommends upper and lower endoscopy for asymptomatic men and postmenopausal women with iron deficiency anemia.

sections.title: After an unrevealing workup
sections.text: For uncomplicated asymptomatic disease after negative endoscopic and noninvasive evaluation, try iron replacement before routine capsule endoscopy.

sections.title: Confirm the blood and iron findings
sections.text: NHLBI lists CBC, hemoglobin, blood iron and ferritin in evaluating suspected iron-deficiency anemia. A symptom such as fatigue does not itself establish the laboratory diagnosis. No ferritin threshold is imported from the page illustration.

sections.title: Diet supports but does not replace etiologic evaluation
sections.text: NHLBI lists iron-containing foods and explains that vitamin-C-rich foods help iron absorption. Dietary counseling can accompany an appropriate treatment and cause-evaluation plan; it does not erase concern for ongoing blood loss.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has confirmed iron deficiency anemia without an obvious bleeding source or gastrointestinal symptoms. Which evaluation is recommended?

choices.text: Routine brain imaging
Bidirectional endoscopy
Iron alone with no cause evaluation
No evaluation because he has no GI symptoms
A stool culture alone

questions.explanation: AGA recommends upper and lower endoscopic evaluation in asymptomatic men with IDA.

distractorExplanations.A: It does not investigate the suspected cause.
distractorExplanations.C: It may miss occult gastrointestinal pathology.
distractorExplanations.D: Asymptomatic men still warrant evaluation.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not evaluate this anemia appropriately.

questions.learningObjective: Investigate unexplained adult iron deficiency despite absent GI symptoms.

questions.stem: An uncomplicated asymptomatic patient has IDA with negative bidirectional endoscopy and noninvasive evaluation. Which next approach generally precedes routine small-bowel capsule testing?

choices.text: Empiric long-term antibiotics
Repeat colonoscopy daily
A trial of iron replacement
Immediate capsule testing in every patient
Stop evaluating and never replace iron

questions.explanation: AGA supports an iron trial before routine capsule evaluation in this selected setting.

distractorExplanations.A: No treatable infection is identified.
distractorExplanations.B: This is not the recommended sequence.
distractorExplanations.D: A replacement trial generally comes first here.
distractorExplanations.E: The deficiency still requires treatment.

questions.learningObjective: Sequence iron treatment after an unrevealing initial GI workup.

questions.stem: A stable patient with fatigue and a history of blood loss is suspected of having iron-deficiency anemia, but no laboratory evaluation has been done. Which initial test set addresses this hypothesis?

choices.text: CBC with hemoglobin and iron studies including ferritin
CBC without an iron or ferritin assessment
Hemoglobin alone without assessing iron stores
Serum iron alone without a blood count or ferritin
CBC with folate testing but no iron studies

questions.explanation: NHLBI lists CBC, hemoglobin, iron and ferritin for diagnosis. This is distinct from the existing question about gastrointestinal cause evaluation after iron deficiency is established.

distractorExplanations.B: It addresses the blood count but omits the iron evaluation needed for the hypothesis supplied.
distractorExplanations.C: It omits the iron and ferritin testing listed by NHLBI for iron-deficiency assessment.
distractorExplanations.D: It does not provide the combined anemia and iron-store evaluation described.
distractorExplanations.E: It omits the iron and ferritin assessment relevant to the proposed diagnosis.

questions.learningObjective: Confirm suspected iron-deficiency anemia before making the laboratory diagnosis.

questions.stem: A patient with confirmed iron deficiency is receiving appropriate treatment and cause evaluation. She asks which food addition is recommended to help absorb iron from meals. Which is most appropriate?

choices.text: Milk as the specific addition recommended to promote iron absorption
Tea with each iron-containing meal as the specific absorption aid
Coffee with each meal as the specific absorption aid
Vitamin-C-rich foods such as oranges or tomatoes
Bran cereal as the specific nutrient addition recommended for iron absorption

questions.explanation: NHLBI explains that vitamin-C-rich foods help the body absorb iron. The stem preserves treatment and investigation of the cause rather than presenting food as a complete anemia treatment.

distractorExplanations.A: NHLBI identifies vitamin-C-rich foods, rather than this choice, for the absorption goal in the question.
distractorExplanations.B: It does not match the vitamin-C food recommendation in the cited reference.
distractorExplanations.C: The source identifies vitamin-C-rich foods for this purpose.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not match the vitamin-C-focused recommendation being tested.

questions.learningObjective: Integrate iron-absorption counseling without abandoning the cause evaluation.

limitations: Accessible AGA society recommendation summary and primary technical-review figure caption; full 2020 guideline access was blocked. No unverified ferritin cutoff is included.
