sections.title: Neurologic recognition
sections.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause neuropathy without anemia; a normal blood count does not exclude neurologic disease.

sections.title: Confirmatory testing
sections.text: Methylmalonic acid can clarify a borderline B12 result; renal impairment also elevates MMA and affects interpretation.

sections.title: Causes and risk
sections.text: Dietary limitation, impaired absorption, intrinsic-factor loss and medications such as metformin contribute; replacement must address the cause.

sections.title: Choose a route that can bypass malabsorption
sections.text: NIH ODS describes parenteral B12 as commonly used for severe deficiency and malabsorption such as pernicious anemia. High-dose oral therapy may also be effective in some settings, with limited evidence. An injection bypasses the gastrointestinal absorption barrier; oral therapy is not universally ineffective.

sections.title: Maternal status matters for the exclusively breastfed infant
sections.text: Exclusively breastfed infants of mothers who consume no animal products can have limited B12 reserves. Maternal deficiency may leave insufficient B12 transfer; untreated infant deficiency can cause developmental delay, poor growth, neurologic damage and anemia.

questions.stem: A patient has distal paresthesias and a borderline serum B12 result. Kidney function is normal. Which test can help confirm functional B12 deficiency?

choices.text: A normal hemoglobin alone
A skin fungal culture
An isolated serum sodium
Serum methylmalonic acid
A urine culture

questions.explanation: MMA helps clarify borderline B12 concentrations; renal function matters in interpretation.

distractorExplanations.A: It cannot exclude neurologic deficiency.
distractorExplanations.B: It does not clarify the B12 result.
distractorExplanations.C: It does not confirm B12 deficiency.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not assess B12 status.

questions.learningObjective: Use MMA appropriately to clarify a borderline B12 level.

questions.stem: A patient on a restrictive diet has neurologic symptoms consistent with B12 deficiency but no anemia. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

choices.text: Normal hemoglobin rules it out
Only patients with macrocytosis can be affected
Dietary history is irrelevant
Symptoms establish the cause without further assessment
B12 deficiency remains possible despite the normal blood count

questions.explanation: Neurologic B12 deficiency is not excluded by absent anemia.

distractorExplanations.A: Neurologic manifestations can occur without anemia.
distractorExplanations.B: Hematologic abnormalities are not required.
distractorExplanations.C: Dietary restriction can increase risk.
distractorExplanations.D: Laboratory and etiologic evaluation are still needed.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize B12-related neurologic disease without anemia.

questions.stem: An adult has severe B12 deficiency with malabsorption. The study question asks which administration route directly bypasses the gastrointestinal absorption barrier. Which answer is correct?

choices.text: A standard-dose oral multivitamin as the sole replacement approach
Parenteral B12, commonly by intramuscular injection
High-dose oral B12
Fortified foods as the sole replacement approach
Dietary animal foods alone

questions.explanation: NIH describes parenteral replacement for severe deficiency and malabsorption. The item asks which route bypasses that barrier, while preserving the possibility of high-dose oral treatment in appropriate cases.

distractorExplanations.A: It does not directly bypass the gastrointestinal route specified.
distractorExplanations.C: NIH notes that high-dose oral treatment can work in some cases, but it does not directly bypass gastrointestinal administration.
distractorExplanations.D: These still use the gastrointestinal route and do not answer the route question.
distractorExplanations.E: These do not directly bypass the gastrointestinal absorption barrier.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a replacement route that bypasses gastrointestinal malabsorption.

questions.stem: An exclusively breastfed infant has poor growth and developmental delay. The mother follows a vegan diet and has untreated documented B12 deficiency. Which nutritional deficiency deserves particular evaluation in the infant?

choices.text: Iron deficiency
Folate deficiency
Vitamin D deficiency
Vitamin B6 deficiency
Vitamin B12 deficiency

questions.explanation: NIH ODS identifies exclusively breastfed infants of mothers consuming no animal products as a risk group and describes developmental and growth harm from infant B12 deficiency. The history supports evaluation, not diagnosis without testing.

distractorExplanations.A: Other causes may be assessed, but the documented maternal B12 deficiency and feeding context identify B12 as the particular concern in this question.
distractorExplanations.B: The documented maternal deficiency and infant risk described by NIH specifically concern B12.
distractorExplanations.C: This does not match the maternal deficiency and infant risk pattern being tested; it does not exclude other nutritional assessment.
distractorExplanations.D: The source identifies infant B12 deficiency as the concern in the supplied maternal and feeding context.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the infant consequence of maternal B12 deficiency.

sections.title: Immediate treatment
sections.text: Epinephrine is first-line for suspected anaphylaxis; do not wait for every diagnostic criterion before treating a concerning evolving reaction.

sections.title: Emergency escalation
sections.text: Severe, persistent, recurrent or worsening symptoms after epinephrine require activation of emergency medical services.

sections.title: Preparation after an episode
sections.text: High-risk patients need accessible autoinjectors and training in recognition, carriage and use; previous multi-dose or biphasic episodes support multiple devices.

sections.title: Resolution does not end monitoring
sections.text: CDC advises transfer to an emergency facility after stabilization of vaccine-associated anaphylaxis and monitoring in a medical facility for several hours, even after complete resolution, because anaphylaxis can recur. This section imports no copyrighted management table or fixed observation duration.

sections.title: Evaluate a prior severe vaccine reaction before repeat dosing
sections.text: In general, a severe allergic reaction to a vaccine is a contraindication to more doses of that vaccine. CDC describes allergist evaluation to identify the responsible component before deciding about the same vaccine or others sharing components. This is not an influenza-specific algorithm.

choices.text: Intramuscular epinephrine
Oral antihistamine alone
Oral corticosteroid before epinephrine
Antibiotics
Observe until every criterion is documented

questions.explanation: Suspected anaphylaxis requires prompt epinephrine.

distractorExplanations.B: It cannot replace first-line epinephrine.
distractorExplanations.C: It delays the priority treatment.
distractorExplanations.D: They do not treat this acute allergic reaction.
distractorExplanations.E: Treatment should not await complete documentation.

questions.learningObjective: Prioritize epinephrine in a multisystem allergic emergency.

questions.stem: A patient previously needed multiple epinephrine doses for anaphylaxis and is planning travel. Which preparation best follows the practice parameter?

choices.text: Give epinephrine daily before any symptoms
Carry multiple prescribed autoinjectors and rehearse use
Carry antihistamines instead of epinephrine
Leave devices home if asymptomatic
Rely on every restaurant stocking epinephrine

questions.explanation: Previous multi-dose anaphylaxis supports access to multiple autoinjectors and practical training.

distractorExplanations.A: Preemptive asymptomatic dosing is not recommended.
distractorExplanations.C: They do not substitute for epinephrine.
distractorExplanations.D: Future exposure is unpredictable.
distractorExplanations.E: Community availability is not assured.

questions.learningObjective: Plan autoinjector access for a patient at high recurrence risk.

questions.stem: A patient with vaccine-associated anaphylaxis has been treated and is now fully stabilized with symptoms resolved. Which disposition best matches the CDC narrative?

choices.text: Discharge as soon as vital signs stabilize without further medical monitoring
End observation when the skin findings resolve
Arrange emergency-facility evaluation and several hours of medical monitoring
Discharge with a telephone check later instead of medical observation
Arrange a next-day outpatient visit as the only further care

questions.explanation: CDC advises emergency-facility transfer after stabilization and several hours of monitoring because anaphylaxis may recur. No exact observation-hour threshold is inferred.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC describes emergency-facility transfer and several hours of monitoring after stabilization.
distractorExplanations.B: Resolution does not remove the additional medical monitoring described by CDC.
distractorExplanations.D: It does not provide the emergency-facility evaluation and monitoring described in the reference.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not provide the several hours of monitoring advised after stabilization.

questions.learningObjective: Preserve observation and further evaluation after initial anaphylaxis resolution.

questions.stem: A patient had a severe immediate allergic reaction to a previous dose of a non-influenza vaccine. Before administering another dose of the same vaccine, which plan is most appropriate?

choices.text: Treat the history as a contraindication pending appropriate specialist evaluation
Give the same vaccine under brief supervision without reviewing the previous reaction
Exclude every vaccine permanently without assessing the responsible component
Reduce the next dose instead of assessing the contraindication history
Premedicate and give the same vaccine without reviewing the reaction

questions.explanation: CDC generally describes a severe vaccine allergic reaction as a contraindication to additional doses of the same vaccine, with allergist evaluation to identify the cause and inform future decisions.

distractorExplanations.B: CDC describes the severe reaction history as a contraindication to additional doses of that vaccine pending appropriate evaluation.
distractorExplanations.C: The reference supports allergist evaluation to identify the cause and inform future vaccine decisions.
distractorExplanations.D: The cited approach is to address the severe reaction history and its cause, rather than substitute dose reduction for evaluation.
distractorExplanations.E: This does not resolve the contraindication history described by CDC.

questions.learningObjective: Use severe vaccine-reaction history in planning later immunization assessment.

sections.title: Initial evaluation
sections.text: Start with a detailed history, examination and resting 12-lead ECG to identify likely causes and high-risk features.

sections.title: Serious associated disease
sections.text: Syncope associated with a serious medical condition warrants hospital evaluation and treatment.

sections.title: Targeted testing
sections.text: Routine broad laboratories, neuroimaging and EEG are not useful defaults; focal neurologic findings or a specific suspicion guide further testing.

sections.title: Match a selected test to postural symptoms
sections.text: MedlinePlus describes tilt-table testing as measuring blood pressure and heart rate during position changes to investigate lightheadedness or fainting. It is a selected evaluation tool, not a routine test required for every first syncope episode.

sections.title: Prevent injury around vaccination
sections.text: CDC advises seated or recumbent vaccination for adolescents and adults. Consider observation while seated or lying for 15 minutes to reduce fainting-injury risk; if syncope occurs, observe until symptoms resolve. This does not replace evaluation of a concerning episode.

questions.stem: A patient presents after a brief faint. History and examination are underway. Which test belongs in the initial syncope evaluation?

choices.text: Broad laboratory panel instead of history
No evaluation after spontaneous recovery
Resting 12-lead ECG
Brain MRI for every faint
EEG for every faint

questions.explanation: The initial assessment includes a resting ECG alongside history and examination.

distractorExplanations.A: Testing does not replace the initial clinical evaluation.
distractorExplanations.B: Recovery does not remove the need to evaluate.
distractorExplanations.D: Routine neuroimaging is not recommended.
distractorExplanations.E: Routine EEG is not recommended.

questions.learningObjective: Identify ECG as part of initial syncope assessment.

questions.stem: A patient has a typical vasovagal episode. Examination and ECG are reassuring; there is no trauma, focal deficit or seizure concern. Which approach is appropriate?

choices.text: Diagnose epilepsy solely because consciousness was lost
Ignore new future high-risk findings
Hospitalize every low-risk vasovagal episode
Education and targeted follow-up without routine neuroimaging or EEG
Routine brain CT and EEG regardless of findings

questions.explanation: Recognized vasovagal syncope supports education; routine neurologic testing is unnecessary in this presentation.

distractorExplanations.A: Transient unconsciousness alone does not establish epilepsy.
distractorExplanations.B: Reassurance does not preclude later reassessment.
distractorExplanations.C: The guideline ties admission to serious associated conditions.
distractorExplanations.E: Absent relevant findings, routine testing is not recommended.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid routine neurologic testing in uncomplicated vasovagal syncope.

questions.stem: After an initial evaluation, a clinician selects further testing of recurrent postural lightheadedness and fainting. Which test directly measures heart rate and blood pressure as the patient’s position changes?

choices.text: A resting 12-lead ECG without postural testing
An ambulatory rhythm recording without a controlled position-change assessment
An echocardiogram without postural blood-pressure measurement
Tilt-table testing
An exercise stress test rather than a tilt assessment

questions.explanation: MedlinePlus explains that tilt-table testing measures blood pressure and heart rate during changes in posture. The stem supplies the decision for a selected further evaluation; it is not a universal first-line test rule.

distractorExplanations.A: It does not provide the direct position-change blood-pressure and heart-rate measurements requested.
distractorExplanations.B: It is not the posture-response test described in the reference.
distractorExplanations.C: It does not provide the specified posture-response measurements.
distractorExplanations.E: The question selects measurement during postural changes, as described for tilt-table testing.

questions.learningObjective: Match tilt-table testing to a selected postural-response evaluation.

questions.stem: An adolescent is about to receive a vaccination and reports fainting after injections in the past. Which precaution best addresses injury prevention according to CDC?

choices.text: Vaccinate standing, then begin seated observation afterward
Vaccinate while seated or lying down and consider 15 minutes of seated or recumbent observation
Vaccinate seated but discharge immediately without considering observation
Use standing observation because the pre-vaccine examination is normal
End observation immediately after a faint while symptoms persist

questions.explanation: CDC advises seated or lying vaccination and consideration of 15-minute observation for adolescents, with observation until symptoms resolve if fainting occurs. This item tests injury prevention rather than the general syncope workup.

distractorExplanations.A: It omits the seated or lying position during vaccination described for injury prevention.
distractorExplanations.C: It omits the observation precaution described for adolescents in this context.
distractorExplanations.D: It does not use the seated or recumbent observation approach recommended to reduce injury risk.
distractorExplanations.E: CDC advises continued observation until symptoms resolve when fainting occurs.

questions.learningObjective: Prevent injury from injection-associated syncope.

sections.title: Individual risk assessment
sections.text: Assess skin, mobility, perfusion and ability to reposition; reassess pressure tolerance as clinical status changes.

sections.title: Repositioning plan
sections.text: Individualize repositioning around tissue tolerance, support surface and goals; a pressure-redistributing mattress does not replace repositioning.

sections.title: Heel offloading
sections.text: At-risk heels should be elevated so they do not contact the support surface; continue broader pressure redistribution and reassessment.

sections.title: Keep skin clean and dry
sections.text: The MedlinePlus summary includes keeping skin clean and dry among pressure-sore prevention measures for people unable to change position. This is one part of a broader pressure-relief plan, not a replacement for offloading or individualized repositioning.

sections.title: Act before an injury advances
sections.text: Pressure sores can lead to serious, sometimes life-threatening infection. The government summary emphasizes early treatment because advanced sores heal slowly. It does not supply wound-staging rules or a specific dressing or antibiotic regimen.

questions.stem: An immobile older adult has vulnerable heel skin. Which intervention specifically reduces continued heel loading?

choices.text: Leave heels pressing against the mattress
Use a mattress as a substitute for all repositioning
Apply antibiotics without infection findings
Stop skin reassessment once equipment arrives
Elevate the heels clear of the support surface

questions.explanation: Heel elevation directly offloads the heel while broader preventive measures continue.

distractorExplanations.A: This retains direct heel pressure.
distractorExplanations.B: Support surfaces do not replace offloading.
distractorExplanations.C: This does not address pressure loading.
distractorExplanations.D: Tissue tolerance needs ongoing reassessment.

questions.learningObjective: Apply heel-specific pressure offloading.

questions.stem: A patient at pressure-injury risk develops early skin damage despite a documented repositioning schedule. What should happen next?

choices.text: Reassess and individualize the repositioning and support-surface plan
Continue the exact schedule without reassessment
Stop repositioning because a special mattress is present
Assume every patient needs an identical interval
Ignore the change until an open wound appears

questions.explanation: New skin damage calls for reassessment of offloading method and frequency.

distractorExplanations.B: New tissue damage warrants reconsideration.
distractorExplanations.C: A mattress does not eliminate repositioning needs.
distractorExplanations.D: Tissue tolerance and clinical needs differ.
distractorExplanations.E: Early damage already merits action.

questions.learningObjective: Adapt prevention when tissue tolerance changes.

questions.stem: A bedridden adult has urinary incontinence and high pressure-injury risk. In addition to the established pressure-relief plan, which skin-care instruction is appropriate?

choices.text: Keep a wet or soiled brief in place until the next scheduled turn
Substitute moisture care for the existing pressure-relief plan
Rely on the support surface while leaving moisture care unaddressed
Use absorbent briefs without regular cleaning of soiled skin
Keep the skin clean and dry

questions.explanation: MedlinePlus includes clean, dry skin in prevention. The question preserves the existing individualized pressure-relief plan rather than importing the summary’s fixed repositioning interval.

distractorExplanations.A: It does not implement the clean, dry skin care described by the reference.
distractorExplanations.B: The question asks for skin care in addition to pressure relief, rather than replacing that plan.
distractorExplanations.C: It omits the skin-care measure identified by MedlinePlus.
distractorExplanations.D: It does not provide the clean, dry skin care specified in the reference.

questions.learningObjective: Add appropriate skin care to a pressure-injury prevention plan.

questions.stem: A wheelchair user notices a new area of pressure-related skin breakdown. Which next step best matches the reference?

choices.text: Adjust prevention measures and assess the wound at the next routine visit
Start an empiric antibiotic before assessing the wound
Arrange early wound assessment and an appropriate treatment plan
Base further assessment on whether the lesion becomes deeper
Continue routine prevention measures until infection symptoms appear

questions.explanation: The MedlinePlus government summary emphasizes early treatment and warns of serious infection. It does not establish a wound stage or a specific treatment prescription.

distractorExplanations.A: Prevention changes do not replace the early assessment and treatment emphasized for existing skin breakdown.
distractorExplanations.B: The reference supports early assessment and treatment but supplies no empiric antibiotic regimen for an unassessed lesion.
distractorExplanations.D: The reference emphasizes early treatment rather than waiting for an advanced sore that may heal slowly.
distractorExplanations.E: The source emphasizes early treatment and warns of serious infection; it does not require infection symptoms before assessing new breakdown.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the value of early pressure-injury assessment.

limitations: International guideline collaboration includes US NPIAP; this module focuses on prevention of further injury rather than complete staging, debridement or infection management.

sections.title: Depth and surface area
sections.text: Superficial redness is excluded from TBSA calculations; partial-thickness and full-thickness injuries contribute to burn area.

sections.title: Referral priority
sections.text: Full-thickness burns, partial-thickness burns involving at least 10% TBSA, or deep burns of key functional areas require immediate consultation and possible transfer.

sections.title: Wound prevention
sections.text: Burns can be dirty/major wounds for tetanus assessment; vaccination history, wound care and immune status guide vaccine and immunoglobulin decisions.

sections.title: Use the dirty/major wound vaccine interval
sections.text: CDC includes burns with devitalized tissue among dirty or major wounds. With a completed tetanus primary series, a booster is indicated when the last dose was 5 or more years ago. No booster is needed if the complete series is documented and the last dose was less than 5 years ago.

sections.title: Unknown history can need vaccine and immunoglobulin
sections.text: For a dirty or major wound with unknown, absent or incomplete tetanus vaccination, CDC indicates both tetanus vaccination and tetanus immune globulin (TIG). Antibiotics are not used solely to prevent tetanus; evaluate and treat actual wound infection separately.

questions.stem: An adult has a 12% TBSA partial-thickness scald burn. Which disposition aligns with ABA referral guidance?

choices.text: Reassure because it is not full thickness
Immediate burn-center consultation with consideration of transfer
Routine follow-up only without consultation
Exclude all partial-thickness areas from TBSA
Wait for infection before consultation

questions.explanation: Partial-thickness burns at or above 10% TBSA warrant immediate consultation and transfer consideration.

distractorExplanations.A: Partial-thickness extent also matters.
distractorExplanations.C: The partial-thickness area meets referral criteria.
distractorExplanations.D: Partial-thickness injuries contribute to TBSA.
distractorExplanations.E: Referral criteria do not require infection.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the partial-thickness burn referral threshold.

questions.stem: A patient has a full-thickness hand burn affecting less than 1% TBSA. What is the appropriate referral approach?

choices.text: Ignore hand function because the area is small
Wait until healing fails before consultation
Immediate burn-center consultation despite the small surface area
No referral because it is below 10% TBSA
Treat as superficial sunburn

questions.explanation: Full-thickness and deep hand burns meet consultation criteria regardless of small size.

distractorExplanations.A: Functional site influences referral.
distractorExplanations.B: Current findings already warrant consultation.
distractorExplanations.D: Depth and hand involvement independently matter.
distractorExplanations.E: The stated depth is full thickness.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize depth and functional-site referral indications.

questions.stem: An adult without HIV or severe immunodeficiency has a burn with devitalized tissue. The tetanus primary series is documented complete, and the last dose was six years ago. What tetanus prevention step is indicated?

choices.text: Give a tetanus vaccine booster
Provide wound care but defer the booster until ten years after the last dose
Use antibiotics instead of tetanus vaccination
Give TIG alone without a vaccine booster
Give vaccine and TIG solely because this is a burn

questions.explanation: CDC treats a burn with devitalized tissue as dirty or major; a completed primary series with the last dose at least 5 years ago calls for a booster. The stem excludes severe immunodeficiency and HIV-related TIG considerations.

distractorExplanations.B: The dirty/major wound booster interval is at least 5 years after the last dose.
distractorExplanations.C: CDC does not recommend antibiotics solely for tetanus prophylaxis.
distractorExplanations.D: The completed-series, six-year interval calls for a booster; this stem excludes the immunodeficiency exceptions for TIG.
distractorExplanations.E: In the supplied completed-series setting without HIV or severe immunodeficiency, the burn indication does not by itself require TIG.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the dirty/major-wound tetanus booster interval in a burn.

questions.stem: An adult has a burn containing devitalized tissue and no reliable tetanus vaccination history. Which tetanus prophylaxis approach follows CDC guidance?

choices.text: Give tetanus vaccine without TIG
Give TIG without starting a vaccination plan
Use antibiotics as the tetanus prophylaxis plan
Tetanus vaccination plus tetanus immune globulin
Provide wound care without tetanus prophylaxis

questions.explanation: For dirty or major wounds and unknown vaccination history, CDC indicates vaccine and TIG. This question adds no product-specific vaccine choice or immunoglobulin dose.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC also indicates TIG for this dirty/major wound with unknown vaccination history.
distractorExplanations.B: CDC indicates vaccination for the unknown history as well.
distractorExplanations.C: Antibiotics do not replace vaccine and TIG in the cited recommendation.
distractorExplanations.E: Unknown vaccination history and devitalized burn tissue meet the cited prophylaxis indications.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the combined tetanus prophylaxis indication with unknown vaccination history.

sections.title: Diagnosis
sections.text: The typical rash often permits clinical recognition; PCR is the most useful laboratory test when confirmation is needed.

sections.title: Early treatment
sections.text: Acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir are preferred antivirals; treatment works best within 72 hours of onset.

sections.title: Vaccination after disease
sections.text: Adults 50 and older still need the recommended two-dose recombinant vaccine after prior zoster; do not vaccinate during an acute episode.

sections.title: An additional vaccine eligibility group
sections.text: CDC recommends two recombinant zoster vaccine doses for adults age 19 years or older who are or will be immunodeficient or immunosuppressed because of disease or therapy. The routine age-50 threshold for immunocompetent adults is not the only eligibility rule.

sections.title: Use lesion PCR when confirmation is needed
sections.text: CDC states that VZV PCR is the most helpful laboratory confirmation test for herpes zoster. Vesicles and scabs are good specimens. Serology has limited value for confirming zoster and is less useful when an appropriate lesion specimen is available.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old has a new painful dermatomal vesicular rash starting yesterday. Which treatment directly addresses acute zoster?

choices.text: Antibiotics alone
Wait several weeks before considering an antiviral
A topical antifungal
An appropriate oral antiviral such as valacyclovir
Shingrix as treatment of the current episode

questions.explanation: Early systemic antiviral therapy is preferred for acute shingles.

distractorExplanations.A: They do not target varicella-zoster virus.
distractorExplanations.B: Early treatment has the greatest benefit.
distractorExplanations.C: It does not treat zoster.
distractorExplanations.E: Vaccination prevents future disease; it is not acute treatment.

questions.learningObjective: Select timely antiviral treatment for acute zoster.

questions.stem: An immunocompetent 62-year-old recovered from shingles and has never received recombinant zoster vaccine. Which recommendation applies?

choices.text: Prior shingles permanently removes vaccine need
Give vaccine only during active vesicles
Use vaccine as an antiviral replacement
Wait until age 80 as a universal requirement
Give the recommended two-dose recombinant zoster vaccine series

questions.explanation: Prior zoster does not remove the age-based recombinant vaccination recommendation.

distractorExplanations.A: Previous disease does not remove the recommendation.
distractorExplanations.B: Avoid vaccination during an acute episode.
distractorExplanations.C: Prevention and acute treatment have different roles.
distractorExplanations.D: Vaccination is recommended starting at age 50.

questions.learningObjective: Apply zoster vaccination after a resolved prior episode.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old receiving immunosuppressive therapy has no current shingles episode and asks whether zoster vaccination must wait until age 50. What is the most appropriate answer?

choices.text: Defer recombinant zoster vaccine until age 50 despite immunosuppression
The immunocompromised recommendation includes adults age 19 and older
Offer recombinant zoster vaccine only after a first shingles episode
Exclude recombinant zoster vaccine consideration throughout immunosuppressive therapy
Use a varicella vaccine as an automatic replacement for the recommended zoster series

questions.explanation: CDC recommends a two-dose recombinant zoster vaccine series for adults at least 19 who are or will be immunodeficient or immunosuppressed. The stem excludes an acute shingles episode.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC includes immunodeficient or immunosuppressed adults age 19 and older.
distractorExplanations.C: A prior shingles episode is not required by the age-and-immunosuppression recommendation supplied.
distractorExplanations.D: The recommendation specifically includes adults who are or will be immunosuppressed, with timing considered appropriately.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not provide the recombinant zoster series in the CDC recommendation being tested.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the younger-adult immunocompromised zoster-vaccine eligibility rule.

questions.stem: An adult has an atypical vesicular eruption, and herpes zoster requires laboratory confirmation. Vesicles and scabs are available for sampling. Which test is most useful?

choices.text: VZV IgM serology as the preferred confirmation despite available lesions
A Tzanck smear instead of PCR on an available skin lesion
Saliva testing instead of sampling the available skin lesions
A serum VZV IgG result as confirmation of the current eruption
VZV PCR from a suitable skin lesion specimen

questions.explanation: CDC recommends PCR as the most helpful confirmation method for zoster, ideally using vesicular material, scabs or cells from the lesion base. The question concerns confirmation of an atypical presentation, not routine testing of every typical rash.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC identifies lesion PCR as the most useful confirmation method for this presentation.
distractorExplanations.B: This does not provide the lesion PCR identified by CDC as most useful for confirming the presentation in this question.
distractorExplanations.C: CDC favors suitable lesion material for PCR in this context.
distractorExplanations.D: It does not provide the direct lesion-based confirmation described by CDC.

questions.learningObjective: Select lesion PCR for an atypical suspected zoster eruption.
